newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH MPS PREPARE FOR FRACTIOUS BUDGET DEBATE.
newsitem.headline: CZECH MPS PREPARE FOR FRACTIOUS BUDGET DEBATE.

text.p: The lower chamber of Czech parliament is expected to begin discussion on the government's proposed 1997 budget as early as Tuesday as partisan bickering over the draft threatens to topple the centre-right government.

The budget's first reading -- proposed as the fifth straight balanced balanced with equal revenue and expenditure of 549.1 billion crowns -- is point six on the agenda which was to begin at 1400 CET (1200 GMT).

The draft must pass three readings before being finally adopted, traditionally in December. The Czech system allows for only detailed adjustments within the agreed principles once the budget gets approval in its first reading.

But the conservative three-party coalition, which came up two seats short of a majority in the house in June elections, is facing stiff demands for support from the centre-left Social Democrats (CSSD) who also chair the budget committee.
"Considering the disunity of the opposition's 101 votes, I hope it will be possible to continue the current transformation programme without any fundamental changes," Klaus told reporters on Tuesday.
Coalition deputies and ministers have raised the stakes on the budget fight saying that if the cabinet's proposal fails, it should be taken as a defacto vote of no confidence.
"It is clear if the budget would not pass, the current governmnet cannot fulfill its functions any more," Labour and Social Affairs Minister Jindrich Vodicka told Reuters.

CSSD has said it wanted the government to tighten measures on tax evasion and economic crime in order to back the draft budget in parliament, as well as halting the planned deregulation of heating prices and state housing rents.

"Oppostion deputies should consider it (whether the budget would pass or not), now they have in their hands the stability of this country," Vodicka, a member of the senior coaliton partner Civic Democratic Party (ODS) added.

The coalition has accused CSSD of joining with the Communists and ultra-right Republicans in parliament to kill the post-Communist reform process, a charge the CSSD and its leader, parliamentary chairman Milos Zeman, vehemently denies.

The debate is taking place in the context of November Senate elections in which analysts believe a strong showing by the coalition of the Social Democrats might spark a call for early elections to the lower house.
ODS and CSSD are virtually deadlocked at just over 25 percent support in recent opinion polls.
Tomas Jezek, an ODS party colleague and former chairman of the budget committee, now the head of Prague Stock Exchange, believes the budget for 1997 will pass in the parliament.
"I think the Social Democrats would not dare to boycott it. The society is very sensitive to someone who causes problems. If they boycott it it could turn against them," Jezek said.
However Jezek said he expects a long debate over the budget before it is finally passed.
